sentences.text: The genus Gilmoreosaurus was formally described by Brett-Surman in 1979 as a group of hadrosauromorphan dinosaurs.
This large hadrosauroid could reach lengths of up to 6.2 meters and weigh between 1.2 and 3.6 tons.
It possessed large lower jaws and long hind legs, yet it lacked the hollow crest found in some relatives.
Fossil specimens include numerous vertebrae, a coracoid bone with a distinct D-shaped glenoid, and a femur featuring a well-developed fourth trochanter.
The right maxilla preserves twenty-six alveolar foramina and twenty-two tooth-filled sockets, though the total tooth count remains unknown due to incomplete fossils.
Tumors such as hemangiomas and metastatic cancer were found in Gilmoreosaurus skeletons, a condition limited to this genus and its close relatives despite examining over 10,000 fossils.
Unlike many modern animals, this dinosaur showed a disappearance of lines of arrested growth, allowing uninterrupted development similar to giant sauropods.
Initial excavations took place over three days in April and May 1922, when George Olsen discovered fossils in quarries located about 14 km northeast of Erenhot.
The type species was originally named Mandschurosaurus mongoliensis in 1923 before being renamed Gilmoreosaurus mongoliensis in 1979.
Gilmoreosaurus likely acted as a medium to low-level browser within its ecosystem.
It likely faced predation from the fast-running tyrannosauroid Alectrosaurus, as their geographic ranges overlapped.
Analysis of bone microstructure suggests Gilmoreosaurus shared similar growth size and rates with other large hadrosauroids like Gobihadros.
The tibia exhibited a decrease in secondary remodelling, an adaptation allowing the bone to bear higher tensions associated with increasing body size.
In 2007, Rothschild and Tanke reported that osteochondrosis was particularly common in rapidly growing hadrosaurs like Gilmoreosaurus.
Researchers suggest the tumors found on caudal vertebrae may have been caused by environmental factors or genetic inheritance.
It is debated whether osteochondrosis was truly absent in Gilmoreosaurus, as the low sample size might have led to false negatives despite the disease being common in other hadrosaurs.
A 2010 study by Prieto-Márquez and Norell placed Gilmoreosaurus in a sister group closely related to Hadrosauridae.
Species G. atavus and G. arkhangelskyi are classified as dubious due to being based on very fragmentary remains.
The type species Gilmoreosaurus mongoliensis lived 96 million years ago in the Iren Dabasu Formation of Inner Mongolia.
It lived during the Cenomanian stage of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 95.8 ± 6.2 million years ago.
Gilmoreosaurus lived from the middle to late Cretaceous, approximately 120 to 70 million years ago, in what is now Asia.

Anatoly K. Rozhdestvensky debated in the 1960s that Bactrosaurus was a hadrosaurine rather than a lambeosaurine, but future authors disagreed and reaffirmed that Bactrosaurus is a lambeosaur distinct from Gilmoreosaurus.
